chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ibn Ri'ab from Abu Ubaydah said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a woman who took medicine while pregnant, and her husband did not know of this, so she miscarried. He said: 'If the fetus has a bone with flesh grown upon it, upon her is a diyah (blood money) which she pays to its father; and if it is a fetus, an 'alaqah (blood clot) or a mudghah (chewed flesh), then upon her is forty dinars or a ghurrah (single adult male/female slave) which she pays to its father.'
I said to him: 'Does she not inherit from her child from the diyah?' He said: 'No, because she killed him, so she does not inherit from him.'

key_terms.دِيَةٌ: Blood money or financial compensation for killing or miscarriage
key_terms.دِيَتِهِ: The blood money/compensation of the child
key_terms.عَلَقَةً: A stage of fetal development, literally a blood clot
key_terms.غُرَّةً: A single adult male or female slave, used as a form of compensation
key_terms.مُضْغَةً: A stage of fetal development, literally a chewed piece of flesh

ai.seo_question: What is the diyah for a miscarriage caused by a pregnant woman's action according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the distinction between 'diyah' (blood money) and 'ghurrah' (compensation for a slave) is applied based on the fetal stage, reflecting the juristic principle that earlier stages of development carry lesser liability. The Imam explicitly links the exclusion of inheritance to the concept of 'qatl' (killing), establishing that the mother, as the direct agent of death, cannot inherit from the child she caused to die, a key nuance in Shia inheritance jurisprudence. This hadith is foundational in the chapter of 'Mirath al-Qatil' (Inheritance of the Killer), illustrating the practical application of the Quranic prohibition on the killer inheriting.
